doc.title: Don Wolff interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 13, 1996

title: Musicians' dignity, jazz in Europe in the 1950s, and Christian McBride
summary: Wolff recalls musicians leaving for Europe, praises their class, and calls jazz America's original art form.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Well one of these days I might. But I do think there’s a certain personal touch when I go to a festival and I know the people who have hand-selected the musicians and then I know I’m going to get what they like and what they like I would normally like or I wouldn’t be there.

One thing I have to say and we have spoken to quite a number of the musicians, and they almost without exception have so much dignity and class that it’s really been inspiring. They have led great lives, certain times have been very difficult for them but boy they just have a lot of dignity.

Well it’s really true. You’re point is very much well taken. And I remember the day in the ‘50s when jazz musicians left the United States because people here didn’t appreciate them. And they had to go to Europe where they were much more appreciated. In fact I was stationed in Europe wearing an Army uniform and had to listen to jazz there in Germany where thousands of people gave standing ovation to the same musicians who were receiving nothing in the way of appreciation back home, and how sad it was I thought that our musicians had to go to Europe to be appreciated. Some of course decided to stay because they didn’t like the way they were being treated because of their color or because they had chosen to become jazz musicians. So it was a very sad period. But today I agree with you. I talk to these musicians and there’s not one of them that’s not willing to share his time and his thoughts and they’re classy, professional people who really enjoy what they do and if you happen to enjoy it just a little bit as much as they then they’re pleased. They certainly don’t do it for the money, because they don’t get well paid.

Well it’s been an inspiration to talk to them. And I’m glad to see that some of the younger musicians like Christian McBride, in addition to doing his own thing, you know he grew up on James Brown, but he recognizes what has come before him and on his first solo record he brings in Ray Brown and Milt Hinton to do a bass trio. I love to see that.

I thought it was very interesting that he did that because it was his way of sharing with the masters, his teacher. And they in turn will do that with him. It’s just an American original art form music. I mean I don’t know how else to better sum it up. Jazz is America’s original art form music. Classical music isn’t, rock & roll isn’t, country music isn’t. Jazz is America’s original art form music.
